messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 30
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bank Teller
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 56

# Vignette: Maya

Maya is a thirty-year-old married woman who works as a bank teller at a mid-sized community branch in the Pacific Northwest. She is soft-spoken, careful with her words, and tends to sit close to the door during sessions. When she first came in, she apologized twice before saying anything of substance. It took several weeks before she was willing to talk about what happened.

Four years ago, Maya was traveling alone in Central America during an extended backpacking trip she had planned since college. She was detained by a small armed faction near a rural border crossing — a case of being in the wrong place, carrying the wrong documents, at the wrong moment. For approximately eleven days, she was held in a concrete structure with no windows. She was subjected to repeated physical violence, sleep deprivation, stress positions, and threats against her family. She describes the experience with a kind of careful flatness, as though narrating something that happened to someone she once knew. She says she learned to leave her body during those days. She still does not fully understand how she was released.

When she returned home, Maya tried to rebuild quietly. She married her long-term partner, Daniel, within the year — a decision she describes as partly motivated by a desperate need to feel anchored to something real. She went back to her job at the bank because it was familiar, because the routine of counting money and greeting customers gave her something to hold onto. For a while, that worked.

But the branch where she works has a back room that staff use for breaks, and it has no windows. Maya has not been inside it in two years. She takes her lunch in her car regardless of the weather, even in January, even in the rain. Her coworkers have stopped asking why.

At the teller window, she is competent and composed, but certain things undo her quickly. A customer who raises his voice. The sound of a door slamming in the back of the branch. The particular smell of concrete dust when maintenance workers are nearby. On three separate occasions she has had to excuse herself mid-transaction, walk to the parking lot, and sit on the curb until she could breathe normally again. She tells herself she is embarrassing. She tells herself she should be over it by now.

At home, she sleeps poorly and lightly. She wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart already running fast, the details of the concrete room more vivid than her own bedroom. Daniel has learned not to touch her when she wakes like that. Early in their marriage he would reach for her, and she would flinch so hard she once knocked him off the bed. She still feels guilty about this. She says she loves him but that she often feels like a stranger living inside her own life, watching herself go through the motions of a normal marriage, a normal job, a normal Tuesday.

She avoids news coverage of political detentions, anything set in Central or South America, and the true crime podcasts she used to love. She has stopped visiting her parents as often because her mother asks questions Maya cannot answer and her father looks at her with an expression she finds unbearable — something between pity and helplessness.

What strikes Maya most, she says, is not the nightmares or the hypervigilance, though those are exhausting. It is the way the experience has fundamentally altered her understanding of the world. She used to believe, in some basic and unexamined way, that safety was the default — that danger was the exception. She no longer believes that. She knows now, in her body and in her bones, that the world can turn on you without warning, without reason, and without remorse. She is not sure how to unknow that. She is not sure it is possible.
